vocabulary.label: Confusing assignment with comparison
vocabulary.description: Using = (which stores a value) where == or === (which compares values) is needed.

vocabulary.label: Mixing up == and ===
vocabulary.description: Treating loose equality (==) and strict equality (===) as interchangeable, when == converts types first.

vocabulary.label: Getting the order of operators wrong
vocabulary.description: Evaluating an expression left to right instead of applying precedence rules.

vocabulary.label: Misjudging truthy and falsy values
vocabulary.description: Assuming a value like 0, "" or [] behaves as true or false when the opposite is the case.

vocabulary.label: Losing track of where a variable exists
vocabulary.description: Expecting a variable declared inside a block or function to be visible outside it.

topics.name: Variables
topics.summary: How to store a value under a name using let, const and var, and when each one is appropriate.

pages.heading: What a Variable Is
Declaring with let
Declaring with const
Naming Variables
pages.body:
A variable name may contain letters, digits, underscores and dollar signs, but it cannot begin with a digit. Names are case sensitive, so score and Score are two different variables.

Good names describe the value: totalMarks is clearer than tm.

pages.heading: The Older var Keyword
pages.body: Older code uses var. A var declaration is visible throughout the whole function that contains it, even before the line where it appears. This behaviour causes confusion, so modern code prefers let and const.

topics.name: Data Types
topics.summary: The basic kinds of value in JavaScript — numbers, strings, booleans, null and undefined — and how to check which one you have.

pages.heading: Numbers
Strings
Booleans
null and undefined
Checking a Type
pages.body:
The typeof operator reports the type of a value as a string.

typeof 7 gives "number"
typeof 'Ana' gives "string"
typeof true gives "boolean"

topics.name: Operators
topics.summary: Arithmetic, assignment and comparison operators, and the order in which JavaScript applies them.

pages.heading: Arithmetic Operators
pages.body:
The arithmetic operators are + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, / for division and % for the remainder.

10 % 3 gives 1, because 3 goes into 10 three times with 1 left over.

pages.heading: The Assignment Operator
Operator Precedence
pages.body:
Multiplication and division are applied before addition and subtraction.

2 + 3 * 4 gives 14, not 20, because 3 * 4 is evaluated first.

Brackets override the order. (2 + 3) * 4 gives 20.

pages.heading: Shorthand Assignment
pages.body:
The shorthand forms combine arithmetic with assignment.

total += 5 means total = total + 5
total -= 2 means total = total - 2

pages.heading: Comparison Operators
pages.body:
Comparison operators produce a boolean. They are > greater than, < less than, >= at least, <= at most, === strictly equal and !== strictly not equal.

7 > 3 gives true.

topics.name: Conditionals
topics.summary: Using if, else if and else to choose between paths, and comparing values correctly with === rather than =.

pages.heading: The if Statement
Comparing Values: = versus ==
pages.body:
This is the most common mistake in this chapter.

A single equals sign assigns. A double or triple equals sign compares.

if (score = 50) is wrong. It stores 50 into score and then treats that as the condition.

if (score === 50) is correct. It asks whether score is 50, and produces true or false.

pages.heading: Strict and Loose Equality
pages.body:
The == operator converts the two values to the same type before comparing. The === operator does not: it requires the same type as well as the same value.

'5' == 5 gives true, because the string is converted to a number.
'5' === 5 gives false, because a string is not a number.

Prefer === so that no hidden conversion happens.

pages.heading: else and else if
Truthy and Falsy Values
pages.body: A condition does not have to be a boolean. JavaScript treats some values as false: 0, the empty string, null, undefined and NaN. Every other value, including the string "0" and an empty array, is treated as true.

pages.heading: Logical Operators
pages.body:
Combine conditions with && for and, || for or, and ! for not.

if (age >= 13 && age <= 19) tests both conditions at once.

topics.name: Loops
topics.summary: Repeating work with for and while loops, and stopping at the right point.

pages.heading: The for Loop
Counting from Zero
pages.body: Loops usually start at 0 because positions in a list start at 0. A loop written with i < length runs exactly length times.

pages.heading: The while Loop
break and continue
pages.body: break leaves the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current pass and starts the next one.

pages.heading: Looping Over a List
pages.body: A for loop can visit every item in a list by using the position as an index, from 0 up to one less than the length.

topics.name: Functions
topics.summary: Packaging code under a name so it can be reused, passing values in and returning a result.

pages.heading: Declaring a Function
Parameters and Arguments
Returning a Value
Function Scope
Arrow Functions
Why Functions Matter
pages.body: Functions let you write a piece of logic once and use it in many places. If the logic needs fixing, you fix it in one spot.

topics.name: Arrays
topics.summary: Storing an ordered list of values and reaching individual items by position.

pages.heading: Creating an Array
pages.body:
An array holds several values in order, written between square brackets.

let marks = [70, 85, 92];

pages.heading: Indexes Start at Zero
pages.body:
The first item is at position 0.

marks[0] gives 70
marks[1] gives 85

The last item is at position length - 1.

pages.heading: Length
pages.body: The length property reports how many items an array holds. For [70, 85, 92], length is 3, and the highest valid index is 2.

pages.heading: Adding and Removing
pages.body: push adds an item to the end. pop removes the last item and gives it back.

pages.heading: Looping Over an Array
pages.body: A for loop from 0 while i < marks.length visits every item exactly once.

topics.name: Objects
topics.summary: Grouping related values together under named keys rather than numbered positions.

pages.heading: Creating an Object
pages.body:
An object groups related values under names, written between braces.

let student = { name: 'Ana', age: 16 };

pages.heading: Reading a Property
pages.body:
Use a dot and the property name.

student.name gives 'Ana'

Square brackets also work when the key is held in a variable.

pages.heading: Changing a Property
Objects Inside Arrays
pages.body: A list of records is usually an array of objects, visited with a loop and read with a dot.

pages.heading: Objects Compared with Arrays
pages.body: Use an array when order matters and the items are the same kind of thing. Use an object when each value means something different and deserves a name.

questions.stem: Which keyword should you use for a value that must never be reassigned?
questions.explanation: const prevents reassignment; assigning to a const throws an error (p.3).

questions.stem: What does `let score = 10;` do?
questions.explanation: A single = stores the value 10 under the name score (p.1).

options.label: A
options.text: Checks whether score is equal to 10

options.label: B
options.text: Stores the value 10 in a variable named score

options.label: C
options.text: Compares score with 10 and returns true or false

options.label: D
options.text: Creates a constant that cannot change

questions.stem: Which variable name is NOT valid in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: A variable name cannot begin with a digit (p.4).

questions.stem: Are `score` and `Score` the same variable?
questions.explanation: Variable names are case sensitive, so these are two different variables (p.4).

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, but only inside a function

options.label: C
options.text: Only if both are declared with const

options.label: D
options.text: No, they are two different variables

questions.stem: Why does modern JavaScript prefer `let` and `const` over `var`?
questions.explanation: A var declaration is visible throughout its whole function, even before its line, which causes confusion (p.5).

options.label: A
options.text: var is visible through the whole function, which is confusing

options.label: C
options.text: var compares values instead of assigning them

questions.stem: How many times do you write `let` for the same variable?
questions.explanation: You write let once, when the variable is first created (p.2).

options.label: A
options.text: Every time you change its value

options.label: B
options.text: Once, when the variable is first created

options.label: C
options.text: Once per function that uses it

options.label: D
options.text: Only when comparing it to another value

questions.stem: What is wrong with `if (score = 50) { ... }`?
questions.explanation: A single = assigns. It stores 50 into score instead of asking whether score is 50. Use === (p.17).

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing — this correctly checks whether score is 50

options.label: B
options.text: The brackets are in the wrong place

options.label: C
options.text: It assigns 50 to score instead of comparing

options.label: D
options.text: score must be declared with const first

questions.stem: Which operator asks whether two values are the same, without converting types?
questions.explanation: === is strict equality: it requires the same type as well as the same value (p.18).

questions.stem: What does `'5' === 5` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Strict equality does not convert types, and a string is not a number (p.18).

options.label: D
options.text: false, because a string is not a number

questions.stem: You want to run code only when `grade` holds the value "A". Which condition is correct?
questions.explanation: Use === to compare. A single = would assign "A" to grade (p.17).

questions.stem: In an if / else if / else chain, how many branches run?
questions.explanation: Only the first matching branch runs (p.19).

options.label: A
options.text: Every branch whose condition is true

options.label: C
options.text: Only the first branch that matches

questions.stem: Which of these values is treated as false in a condition?
questions.explanation: The falsy values are 0, the empty string, null, undefined and NaN. "0" and [] are truthy (p.20).

questions.stem: What does the `return` keyword do?
questions.explanation: return sends a value back to whoever called the function (p.29).

options.label: A
options.text: Sends a value back to the caller

options.label: B
options.text: Prints a value to the console

options.label: C
options.text: Restarts the function from the top

options.label: D
options.text: Stores the value in a global variable

questions.stem: A variable declared with `let` inside a function can be used where?
questions.explanation: It exists only inside that function; code outside cannot see it (p.30).

options.label: B
options.text: Anywhere after the function is declared

options.label: D
options.text: Only inside loops within that function

questions.stem: In `function greet(name) { ... }`, what is `name`?
questions.explanation: A parameter is the name in the declaration; the value passed at the call is the argument (p.28).

questions.stem: What does `double(4)` give, if `function double(n) { return n * 2; }`?
questions.explanation: The function returns n * 2, so 4 * 2 is 8 (p.29).

questions.stem: What happens to code written after a `return` statement?
questions.explanation: Code after a return never runs (p.29).

options.label: C
options.text: It runs only if the return value is false

options.label: D
options.text: It runs in the calling function instead

questions.stem: What does the arrow function `const double = (n) => n * 2;` return?
questions.explanation: When the body is a single expression, its value is returned automatically (p.31).

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing, it needs an explicit return

questions.stem: What does `typeof 7` give?
questions.explanation: typeof reports the type as a string; for 7 that is "number" (p.10).

questions.stem: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined`?
questions.explanation: undefined means never given a value; null means deliberately given "no value" (p.9).

options.label: B
options.text: undefined was never set; null was set to "no value"

options.label: C
options.text: null is zero and undefined is an empty string

questions.stem: Which of these is a boolean?
questions.explanation: A boolean is either true or false (p.8).

questions.stem: What does `2 + 3 * 4` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Multiplication is applied before addition, so 3 * 4 is evaluated first (p.13).

questions.stem: What does `10 % 3` give?
questions.explanation: % is the remainder: 3 goes into 10 three times with 1 left over (p.11).

questions.stem: What does `total += 5` mean?
questions.explanation: The shorthand += combines addition with assignment (p.14).

options.label: D
options.text: Adds 5 only if total is already true

questions.stem: How many times does `for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++)` repeat?
questions.explanation: It runs while i is less than 5, starting at 0 — five passes (p.22).

questions.stem: What does `break` do inside a loop?
questions.explanation: break leaves the loop immediately (p.25).

options.label: D
options.text: Pauses until the condition is true

questions.stem: Why must something inside a `while` loop change the condition?
questions.explanation: Otherwise the condition stays true and the loop never ends (p.24).

options.label: D
options.text: Otherwise the operators are applied backwards

questions.stem: For `let marks = [70, 85, 92];`, what does `marks[1]` give?
questions.explanation: Indexes start at 0, so position 1 is the second item (p.34).

questions.stem: For an array of length 3, what is the highest valid index?
questions.explanation: The highest index is length - 1, which is 2 (p.35).

questions.stem: What does `pop` do?
questions.explanation: pop removes the last item and gives it back (p.36).

options.label: A
options.text: Adds an item to the end

options.label: D
options.text: Removes the last item and returns it

questions.stem: For `let student = { name: 'Ana', age: 16 };`, how do you read the name?
questions.explanation: Use a dot and the property name (p.39).

questions.stem: What happens with `student.grade = "A";` when `grade` does not exist yet?
questions.explanation: Assigning to a property that does not exist adds it (p.40).

questions.stem: When should you use an object rather than an array?
questions.explanation: Use an object when each value means something different and deserves a name (p.42).

options.label: A
options.text: When the items are in a strict order

options.label: B
options.text: When there are more than ten items

options.label: C
options.text: When each value means something different

options.label: D
options.text: When the values are all numbers
